newsitem.title: INDIA: Key India parties to seek changes in 97/98 budget.
newsitem.headline: Key India parties to seek changes in 97/98 budget.

text.p: India's four leading left-wing parties on Monday urged Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's government to modify the 1997/98 (April-March) budget, due to be taken up by parliament this week.

The rightwing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), in a separate move, said it would also oppose certain proposals in the budget presented in parliament on February 28 by former finance minister P. Chidambaram.
Gujral's cabinet last week adopted Chidambaram's budget but left it open to changes by crucial allies when it is taken up in parliament.
The Left Front issued a statement after a meeting calling for changes in the areas of insurance, taxes, divestment in state enterprises, public distribution, customs duties and excise duties.

"The Left parties are of the considered opinion that certain changes are required in the budget proposals and Finance Bill which will be in keeping with the interests of the people and the country," the group said.
The Left Front comprises the two main communist parties, the Revolutionary Socialist Party and the Forward Bloc, all components of Gujral's United Front coalition.
The parties said they were opposed to opening up the health insurance sector to private firms.

"In the interests of strengthening the public sector, the proposal for disinvestment of the PSU (public sector unit) shares in the profitable units and in core and strategic areas should not be proceeded with," it added.
The budget, widely applauded by economists when it was unveiled in February by the previous administration of H.D. Deve Gowda, was due to be taken up by parliament in a session starting on Wednesday.

"This government is seeking to increase the cost of sanitary napkins and samosas with unfair excise levies, but it wants to make imports of luxury items cheaper," former BJP president Murli Manohar Joshi told Reuters.
Joshi was referring to a higher tax on cooking oil used for making samosas, fried vegetable patties popular in northern India.
"We are considering cut motions on the budget. We'll decide which aspects of the budget we want the government to amend," he said.
Chidambaram's proposals on income tax cuts have been accepted by the BJP. But the Congress party and the Left Front, Gujral's crucial allies, were opposed to the reductions.

"We want to amend the budget proposals on the two higher income groups," said Sitaram Yechury, politburo member of the Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M). "The reduction in tax on the lower income groups is, however, acceptable to us."
Chidambaram had proposed reducing the tax rate on annual income between 40,000 rupees ($1,120) and 60,000 rupees to 10 percent from 15 percent.

The tax rate on income between 60,000 and 150,000 rupees would be cut to 20 percent from 30 percent, while the rate on incomes above 150,000 rupees would be reduced to 30 percent from 40. ($1=35.75 rupees)
